content.text: Family Law & Child Support Attorney Serving the Rio Grande Valley Divorce, child custody battles, and disputes over child support—these are some of life’s most challenging and emotionally fraught experiences. If you face a family law issue, the weight of the decisions before you can feel overwhelming. How will this impact your children? Your finances? Your future? In trying times like these, you need a trusted legal partner who understands what you’re going through and has the knowledge and experience to protect your interests. At the family law and child support law firm Garza Law Office, PLLC, we’ve been helping families in Edinburg and throughout the Rio Grande Valley navigate complex family law matters for years. We know that no two families or situations are alike. That’s why we take the time to really listen to you, understand your unique needs and goals, and craft a legal strategy tailored just for you. Comprehensive Family Law Services Our experienced family law attorney can assist you with all aspects of your case, including: Divorce: We’re prepared to advocate fiercely on your behalf whether you anticipate an amicable, uncontested divorce or a complicated battle over assets and child custody. We’ll work to achieve a fair property division and develop a parenting plan that safeguards your children’s best interests. Child Custody and Visitation: As a parent, your top priority is your children’s well-being. We’ll help you establish or modify custody and visitation arrangements that protect your parental rights and foster your children’s healthy development. When necessary, we’re prepared to litigate aggressively to preserve your parent-child relationship. Child Support: Both parents share a legal and ethical duty to financially support their children. We can help you secure a child support order that accurately reflects your children’s needs and the other parent’s ability to pay, following Texas’s child support guidelines. If you’re a parent who is owed child support arrears, we can also assist you in enforcing the order. Spousal Maintenance: Depending on the length of your marriage and the financial circumstances, you may be entitled to spousal support, known as spousal maintenance, in Texas. Our family law attorneys will assess your situation and, when appropriate, pursue spousal maintenance that allows you to maintain your standard of living as you transition to the next chapter of your life. Modifications: Even after your divorce is finalized, changing life circumstances may necessitate revisiting the terms of your divorce decree. Whether you’ve experienced a significant change in income, need to relocate for a job, or have other reasons to request a post-divorce modification, our team will guide you through the process and protect your interests. Texas Family Law: What You Need to Know Family law is complex, and the rules vary from state to state. Here are a few key things to understand about Texas family law and how it may impact your case: Property Division Texas is a community property state. This means that any assets or debts acquired during the marriage are presumed to be owned equally by both spouses and subject to division upon divorce. However, there are exceptions for separate property, such as property owned prior to marriage or inheritance. (Tex. Fam. Code § 7.001) In a divorce, the court will divide the community estate in a “just and right” manner, taking into account various factors, including each spouse’s earning capacity, custody of children, and fault in the divorce. Child Custody In Texas, child custody is known as “conservatorship.” The court’s primary concern in determining conservatorship is the child’s best interests. There is a rebuttable presumption that joint managing conservatorship (similar to joint custody) is in the child’s best interests. (Tex. Fam. Code § 153.131) However, if there is a history of family violence or abuse, the court will typically award sole managing conservatorship to the non-abusive parent. Child Support Texas uses a formula to calculate guideline child support based on the non-custodial parent’s net resources and number of children. The court can deviate from guideline support for a variety of reasons, such as if the child has special needs or to account for the custody/visitation schedule.
